# Unfair dismissal

Learn about the steps an employee can take if they believe their termination is unfair.

## On this page:

- [Unfair dismissal](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/ending-employment/help-with-termination/unfair-dismissal#unfair-dismissal)
- [Applying for unfair dismissal](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/ending-employment/help-with-termination/unfair-dismissal#applying-for-unfair-dismissal)
- [Small business employers](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/ending-employment/help-with-termination/unfair-dismissal#small-business-employers)
- [Other dismissals](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/ending-employment/help-with-termination/unfair-dismissal#other-dismissals)

## Unfair dismissal

Unfair dismissal is when an employee is dismissed from their job in a way that is:

- harsh, unjust, or unreasonable
- not a genuine [redundancyWhen an employee is terminated because the employer no longer requires that job to be done by anyone, except in cases of ordinary and customary turnover of staff. Other known terms: retrenchment and severance pay.](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/taxonomy/term/401 "redundancy"), and
- if the employer is a [small businessA small business employer is an employer with fewer than 15 employees at a particular time. If an employer has 15 or more employees at a particular time, they are no longer a small business employer. When counting the number of employees, employees of associated entities of the employer are included. Casual employees are not included unless engaged on a regular and systematic basis.](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/taxonomy/term/527 "small business employer"), not consistent with the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code.

### Tip: Different dismissal rules for small businesses

The Small Business Fair Dismissal Code helps small business employers follow a fair dismissal process.

Download the [Small Business Fair Dismissal Code and checklist](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/sites/default/files/migration/715/Small-Business-Fair-Dismissal-Code-2011.docx "Small Business Fair Dismissal Code & Checklist") [Small Business Fair Dismissal Code and checklist](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/sites/default/files/migration/715/Small-Business-Fair-Dismissal-Code-2011.pdf "Small Business Fair Dismissal Code & Checklist").

The Fair Work Commission (Commission) decides on cases of unfair dismissal and can issue an order or a decision with the outcome. When deciding if a dismissal was harsh, unjust, or unreasonable, they must consider several factors. These include:

- whether there was a valid reason for the dismissal relating to the employee's capacity or conduct
- whether the employee was given a reason for the dismissal and a chance to respond
- if the dismissal was due to underperformance, whether the employee had been warned about their performance before the dismissal.

If the Commission decides the dismissal was unfair, they may order reinstatement or compensation.

For more information, visit the Commission's website at [Unfair dismissal](https://www.fwc.gov.au/job-loss-or-dismissal/unfair-dismissal).

### What counts as dismissal?

‘Dismissal’ is when employment ends because of a decision by the employer. Not all dismissals are unfair.

In some cases, if the employer's behaviour forces an employee to resign, that might also be a dismissal. This is often called [constructive dismissalWhere an employee quits but was forced to do so because of the conduct of their employer.](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/taxonomy/term/510 "constructive dismissal").

To learn more, go to the Commission's website at [What is unfair dismissal?](https://www.fwc.gov.au/job-loss-or-dismissal/unfair-dismissal/about-unfair-dismissal/what-unfair-dismissal)

## Applying for unfair dismissal

We don’t investigate unfair dismissal complaints.

If you think you’ve been unfairly dismissed, you can apply to the Commission for unfair dismissal. You need to apply to the Commission within 21 days of your dismissal.

To be eligible to apply for unfair dismissal, you must:

- have worked for that employer for at least 6 months, or 12 months if you worked for a [small businessA small business employer is an employer with fewer than 15 employees at a particular time. If an employer has 15 or more employees at a particular time, they are no longer a small business employer. When counting the number of employees, employees of associated entities of the employer are included. Casual employees are not included unless engaged on a regular and systematic basis.](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/taxonomy/term/527 "small business employer")
- be covered by the [national workplace relations system](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/about-us/workplace-laws/fair-work-system#who-is-covered "Fair Work system")
- be covered by an award or enterprise agreement or earn less than the [high income threshold](https://library.fairwork.gov.au/viewer/?krn=K600486).

If there was a change of business ownership, service with the first employer may count as service with the second employer when calculating the minimum employment period.

Check whether you can apply for unfair dismissal with the [Commission’s eligibility quiz](https://www.fwc.gov.au/job-loss-or-dismissal/unfair-dismissal/apply).

### Example: Applying for unfair dismissal

Josie has worked as a part-time barista at a cafe for 2 years. During her shift, her manager tells her that this is her last shift and not to come in tomorrow.

Josie asks why her employment is ending and her manager says it’s because they’re not happy with her performance. Josie is surprised by this as she hasn’t been given any warnings or feedback about her performance.

Josie checks the Commission’s [unfair dismissal eligibility quiz](https://www.fwc.gov.au/job-loss-or-dismissal/unfair-dismissal/about-unfair-dismissal/check-eligibility-unfair-dismissal) and learns she is eligible to lodge an unfair dismissal application. She also learns that she must lodge her application within 21 days of her dismissal.

Visit the Commission's website to:

- learn more about [unfair dismissal](https://www.fwc.gov.au/job-loss-or-dismissal/unfair-dismissal)
- find out [how to lodge the application form](https://www.fwc.gov.au/form/apply-unfair-dismissal-form-f2)
- if you’re eligible, access [free legal advice about unfair dismissal](https://www.fwc.gov.au/apply-or-lodge/legal-help-and-representation/legal-advice-workplace-advice-service).

## Small business employers

A small business employer is any business with less than 15 employees.

The unfair dismissal rules apply to small business employers, but some rules apply differently. For example, employees of a small business can only apply for unfair dismissal after their first 12 months of employment.

The [Small Business Fair Dismissal Code](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/sites/default/files/migration/715/Small-Business-Fair-Dismissal-Code-2011.docx "Small Business Fair Dismissal Code & Checklist") [Small Business Fair Dismissal Code](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/sites/default/files/migration/715/Small-Business-Fair-Dismissal-Code-2011.pdf "Small Business Fair Dismissal Code & Checklist") (the Code) applies to small business employers. If an employee is dismissed and the employer has followed the Code, then the dismissal will be considered to be fair.

To work out whether a business is a small business, count all employees employed by the business including:

- the employee and any other employees being dismissed at that time
- casual employees employed on a regular and systematic basis by the business
- employees of [associated entitiesAssociated entities are businesses or other bodies that are connected to each other in some way. For example, when 1 business owns or controls the other business for the purpose of a transfer of business. Section 50AAA of the Corporations Act provides a full definition.](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/taxonomy/term/487 "associated entities"), including those based overseas.

When checking if a business is a small business for unfair dismissal, the size of the business is counted at the earliest of the following times:

- when the employee is given their [notice of termination,](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/ending-employment/dismissal "Dismissal") or
- when the employment ends (for example, where the employee was not entitled to notice of termination).

### Example: Following the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code

Karolina runs a small pharmacy and has 8 employees. Jason has been working for Karolina as a full-time pharmacy assistant for over a year.

Recently, Karolina has had some serious concerns about Jason's work attendance. Over the past month, Jason has been getting to work up to 45 minutes late and taking unauthorised breaks multiple times a day. This has been negatively impacting on customer service and increasing pressure on other staff.

Karolina has had an informal discussion with Jason about the issues, but Jason doesn't provide any explanation for his behaviour and continues to arrive late and take unapproved breaks.

After considering her options, Karolina feels that she may need to dismiss Jason to prevent further impacts on her business and so that she can hire someone more reliable. She learns about our Small Business Showcase and the information available to her. This includes:

- the [Small Business Fair Dismissal Code](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/sites/default/files/migration/715/Small-Business-Fair-Dismissal-Code-2011.docx "Small Business Fair Dismissal Code & Checklist") [Small Business Fair Dismissal Code](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/sites/default/files/migration/715/Small-Business-Fair-Dismissal-Code-2011.pdf "Small Business Fair Dismissal Code & Checklist")
- a manager’s online course about [Difficult conversations in the workplace](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/tools-and-resources/online-learning-centre/difficult-conversations-in-the-workplace-manager-course "Difficult conversations in the workplace - manager course")
- templates to help with [performance management and issuing warnings](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/tools-and-resources/templates#managing "Templates").

Karolina uses this information and follows the steps in the Code. This includes providing Jason with a warning that he is at risk of dismissal and an opportunity to change his behaviour. After seeing no improvement, Karolina dismisses him.

She saves a copy of the Code and other documents related to Jason's performance. Karolina knows she may need to show the Commission she followed the Code if an unfair dismissal claim is made.

## Other dismissals

Employees can also apply to the Commission if they’ve been dismissed because of:

- a reason prohibited by the general protections, or
- unlawful termination.

For more information, visit [Protections at work](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/employment-conditions/protections-at-work "Protections at work").

[Regulated workersA person who is an employee-like worker or a regulated road transport contractor.](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/taxonomy/term/795 "regulated worker") can apply to the Commission for a remedy for unfair deactivation or unfair termination. For more information, go to the Commission's website at [Unfair deactivation or termination for regulated workers](https://www.fwc.gov.au/job-loss-or-dismissal/unfair-deactivation-or-termination-regulated-workers).

Source reference for page: [Fair Work Act 2009 sections 23, 382–388, 394](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2009A00028/latest/text)
